opus-5.5.text:
Living in New York has made the gap between AI research and the actual world feel very concrete. In the Bay Area, almost everyone you meet works in tech, so it's easy to believe the most important problems are the ones on the leaderboards. In New York, I take the subway, walk through crowded streets, and talk to people in finance, art, medicine, and fashion, and most of them don't care about benchmark numbers. They care whether something actually helps them.

That has shifted how I think about intelligence. The city is a messy, dense, physical environment. You have to read people's body language, avoid a bike coming at you, find your way when the train is rerouted. Humans handle this effortlessly, and none of it comes from reading text. It comes from seeing, moving, and having a model of how the world works. Our current systems are extremely good with language, but they're still quite weak at that grounded, spatial, everyday understanding. Walking around New York reminds me every day how much is missing.

So my sense is that researchers should look up from the screen a bit. Some of the most interesting open problems are in visual and spatial intelligence, world models, and systems that can perceive and act in real environments, not just predict the next token.

There's also a cultural side. New York doesn't have one dominant industry, so you don't feel pressure to follow one narrative. That gives you room to work on things that are unfashionable or long-term. Academia here can afford to be a little contrarian. I think that's healthy, because the field needs people exploring different directions, not everyone converging on the same recipe.

r001.rationale: The speaker says walking New York makes the gap between AI research and the actual world concrete, connecting research to everyday settings.

r002.rationale: The response says most people do not care about benchmark numbers and care whether tools help them, but does not say AI may eventually affect people who have no interest in AI.

r003.rationale: It recommends that researchers focus on real-world usefulness, but does not raise whether AI researchers have social responsibilities.

r004.rationale: The speaker describes conversations with people in several fields as part of a shift toward building AI with grounded spatial intelligence and the ability to act in real environments.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, because New York really did change me. Before I came to NYU, I spent years in industry labs where the day-to-day rhythm was very internal. You talk to colleagues, you read papers, you run experiments, and the "world" is mostly benchmarks and leaderboards. Moving to a city like New York, where you walk everywhere, take the subway, and bump into people from every background imaginable, you start to notice how little of real life actually looks like a benchmark.

I think the first thing it taught me is humility about what we call "vision." When I walk down the street, the problems are not "classify this image into one of a thousand categories." They are things like: understanding a crowded, messy scene; reasoning about what a person on a bike is about to do; reading a hand-written sign in a shop window that's half covered; dealing with rain, glare, construction, and chaos. Everyday life is long-tailed, ambiguous, and constantly changing. That pushed me toward caring much more about representations that are robust and general, rather than squeezing another half-point out of a curated dataset.

The second thing is about who we build for. In an industry lab it's easy to optimize for what's measurable and what scales. In New York you see people who use technology in very different ways, and a lot of them are not the people who show up in our training data or our user studies. That made me think that researchers, especially in academia, have a responsibility to work on the unglamorous but foundational problems: how to understand the physical world, how to make models that are open and reproducible so others can build on them, how to make the science itself healthier. Those are things that are hard to justify quarter to quarter in a company, but a university is exactly the place for them.

And the third thing is simply that the city keeps you honest about hype. You can read online that AGI is around the corner, then you go outside and the subway is late, the delivery robot is stuck on a curb, and a tourist is asking you for directions a phone couldn't give them. The gap between what our models can do in a demo and what they can do in the messy real world is still very large. For me, that gap is where researchers should be. Not chasing the next flashy result, but patiently working on perception, reasoning, and grounding so that one day the system actually understands the world the way a person walking through Manhattan does. New York makes that gap visible every single day, and I find that motivating rather than discouraging.

r001.rationale: The speaker contrasts isolated work on benchmarks with walking through New York and encountering people from many backgrounds, which reveals how unlike everyday life benchmarks are.

r002.rationale: The response discusses people who are underrepresented in training data and user studies, but does not say AI may affect people who have no interest in AI.

r003.rationale: The speaker explicitly says researchers, especially in academia, have a responsibility to address foundational problems.

r004.rationale: The speaker says seeing how people in New York use technology reshaped who researchers should build for and motivated work on robust, open, grounded models.

astra-6.text:
I think living in New York makes it harder to think of intelligence as just a benchmark score. You’re surrounded by people doing very different kinds of work, with different constraints and different ideas of what would actually make their lives better. That’s a useful reminder for an AI researcher: the problems we find interesting aren’t automatically the problems people need solved.

It also makes me think about the gap between a demonstration and something useful. In research, you can show that a model succeeds on a task. In everyday life, people need to know whether they can depend on it, whether correcting its mistakes takes more effort than doing the task themselves, and whether it fits into how they work.

I don’t think that means we should stop pursuing fundamental research. But we should keep asking what our progress means outside our own community. Does it give someone more time? Does it make something easier to understand or more accessible? Those questions should help shape what we choose to work on.

r001.rationale: The response says living in New York exposes the speaker to people with different work and needs, but it does not describe walking through the city or explicitly breaking down a separation from everyday life.

r002.rationale: It discusses solving problems people need addressed and progress beyond the AI research community, but does not say AI may affect people who have no interest in AI.

r003.rationale: The response urges researchers to consider progress outside their community, but does not raise whether they have social responsibilities.

r004.rationale: The speaker says living among people with varied work and constraints is a useful reminder that research should address real needs, and that such questions should shape what researchers work on.

sol-6.1.text:
Living in New York reminds me how much of life happens outside the problems we choose to study. You walk down the street, take the subway, interact with people who have very different experiences, and you realize that a benchmark captures such a small part of the world.

For me, that raises a question: are we working on something because it matters, or because we know how to measure progress on it? We need benchmarks, of course. But we also need to step back and ask whose problems we’re solving and what it would mean for a system to be useful in their everyday lives.

I think being a researcher means protecting time for fundamental questions while staying curious about the world beyond the lab. A city like New York is a good reminder to do both.

r001.rationale: The speaker says walking through the city and meeting people with different experiences shows how little benchmarks capture, connecting everyday life to work beyond the lab.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that AI may affect people who have no interest in AI.

r003.rationale: It asks whose problems researchers are solving and whether their work matters, but does not clearly raise the question of researchers’ social responsibilities.

r004.rationale: The speaker connects encounters with people in everyday life to asking whose problems AI systems should address and how they can be useful in daily life.
